Take a look at sentiment right now.

Because of a personal event involving Jensen Huang, there are now widespread calls that the "AI bubble has popped."

Sentiment is as though AI has failed, the investment wave is over, and we are in a global depression.

In reality? The S&P 500 is up +7% YTD, +60% in 5 years, and ~7% away from a record high, with US AI CapEx running at over $1 trillion per year.

Meanwhile, AI-associated sectors and tech investments have accounted for ~44% of total US GDP growth on a rolling four-quarter basis.

And, Nvidia, $NVDA, is guiding nearly $750 billion in revenue for next year, even without Jensen Huang.

The underlying fundamentals of the AI Revolution have not suddenly deteriorated because of a leadership crisis at one company.

The unfortunate result of this drawdown, as with nearly every other correction since the AI Revolution began, will be countless investors getting crushed on the way back up.

Today's fearmongers become tomorrow's short squeeze as soon as sentiment shifts again.

The comments on this post will be a perfect example of just how polarized sentiment has become in the "doom" direction.

Asset owners will win and the AI Revolution is far from over.

Recency bias will tell you that breakouts are failing, with lots of chop and not dependable. Better to wait for a pullback.

Then you look at earlier breakouts and conclude that the best time is to act at the time of the breakout as you might not be able to capture the strongest moves.

Which one are you going with? 

1) Act at the time of the breakout
2) Wait for a pullback, market will chop and given another opportunity

For those who look at a chart and say "no way" "impossible" "in your dreams"

Remember that in financial markets to remain solvent you need to always expect the unexpected. Which means you need to always be open minded and have a plan.

If that plan is a stop loss, moving cash into T-bills, shifting money to another broker account or as in Marty Schwartz's case carrying the gold home... you need to have one. 

Crashes and bankruptcies happen once.

An example from day to day life you can't imagine how many times I warned people around me to lock their doors during their 5 min hop off to a supermarket to "quickly" buy things. 

Thefts do not take 1 hour. It happens quickly.

In Pit Bull: Lessons from Wall Street's Champion Trader Martin Schwartz's autobiography: 

Going for the Gold I

In August 1982, Schwartz hears that Mexico may default on its debt and that US banks could face a run. He panics and sends his wife Audrey to retrieve his gold Krugerrands and Maple Leafs from the bank before it closes.

She brings home a briefcase full of gold worth over $100,000.

Going for the Gold II

During another financial scare, he again rushes to retrieve his gold from a bank safe-deposit box. He describes carrying approximately 40 pounds of gold coins, worth at least $250,000.

He writes:

“Twice now, I'd gone for the gold.”

There is a lot of discussion today about AI recruitment. Is it all bots?

Here is how OJ is currently recruiting:

After putting out a public notice to gather proposals for an analyst, we evaluated them but then also three of us personally drove to a local Ivy League business MBA program, sat down for meetings, and talked with graduates over coffee.

That was super high signal.

After that, we followed up, and they excited our other partners in a zoom interview, or didn’t. The right people can assert themselves across multiple mediums. We’re highly engaged for super-interested talent only.

My takeaways:
-Elite employers are of course recruiting face to face. People will travel for talent, as we did.
-Elite colleges matter. Speaking for ourselves, we go to the best.
-But I was a trailer park kid. I went to state schools. I was never Ivy.
-OJ seeks out extraordinary enthusiasm and talent, but doesn’t care where it comes from if excellence is demonstrated. If someone has an extraordinary story and wants to work for us, let us know.
https://t.co/tLu7vEvP6y 

We seek to find talent in all forms, while warning that the baseline is very high.
